senses.gloss:
puṣyasnāna
(‘bath during the presence of the नक्षत्र पुष्य’)
------------------------------------------
If there are evil forces in nature manoeuvred by goblins and ghosts to disturb the peace of man, there are also supernatural remedies, good enough to neutralise them or even frighten them away! This was the discovery of the ancient ṛṣis or the sages of India. The remedies they have prescribed go by the general name ‘śānti’.
Out of several such शान्तिस् prescribed by them, the पुष्यस्नान (or puṣyābhi-ṣeka) is also one.
Bṛhaspati, the गुरु or the teacher of the gods, is said to have performed this śānti rite for इन्द्र, the king of gods. Hence it is also known as ‘bārhaspatya-स्नान’.
This rite is reserved for the kings, whose well-being is of primary importance for the welfare of the whole country ruled by them.
Though it may be performed on any day that is associated with the पुष्य नक्षत्र, the pūrṇimā or the full-मोओन् day is the best.
The Bṛhatsaṁhitā (47.1-87) of वराहमिहिर (6th century A. D.) and the Viṣṇudharmottarapurāṇa (2.103) give a fairly detailed description of this rite.
Some of the more important steps of this rite may now be listed as follows:
Choosing a proper date; selecting a suitable spot for the performance of this rite which should be full of trees and plants with fragrant flowers as also ponds inhabited by swans; drawing a मण्डल (geometrical diagram of mystical significance) to keep the various articles needed for the rite; ceremonially establishing the fire for offering oblations with appropriate mantras; होम proper; seating the king on a golden throne at a suitable place in the site of the ritual; sprinkling clarified butter and holy water from the kalaśas (sacred pots) on him with mantras to purify him; the king taking a ceremonial bath and then wearing two special (cotton) garments for the occasion; special oblations into the fire for the welfare of the king; the king honouring all the priests involved in the rite; release of animals meant for slaughter; release of all prisoners except those who have tried to harm him or rebelled against him.
Sometimes, the पुष्यस्नान has been described as a part of लक्षहोम also.

pustaka
(‘book’)
------------------------------------------
The various gods and goddesses of the Hindu pantheon are often shown with āyudhas (weapons or implements) in their hands. One such आयुध, of the sāttvika type, is the पुस्तक (a book, a manuscript).
The gods in whose hand this is shown are: ब्रह्मा, दक्षिणामूर्ति, गणपति, हनुमान्, हयग्रीव, सरस्वती and the sage व्यास.
It symbolises the āgama or the scriptures.
The other objects that generally go with it are the अक्षमाला (rosary), the कमण्डलु (water pot) and the jñānamudra or the gesture of exposition.

Pūṣan
(‘the nourisher’)
------------------------------------------
Pūṣan (or Pūṣā) is one of the twelve aspects of the Sun, known as the Ādityas or Dvādaśādityas. He represents the nourishing and life-supporting aspect of the Sun. He is exceedingly beautiful. He wears a चक्र or a discus with which he destroys the evil ones. He is ever eager to protect his votaries. He looks upon all with an equal eye and is very generous.
He has been eulogised in eight sūktas of the Ṛgveda (3.62.9; 6.53.3; 6.58.3; 10.17.5).
According to paurāṇic legends, he was present at the sacrifice of दक्ष. When वीरभद्र, an emanation from रुद्र/Śiva, attacked and destroyed दक्ष’s sacrifice, पूषन् was one of the victims who lost his teeth (vide Bhāgavata 4.5.21).
See also ĀDITYAS.

Puṣpaka
(‘that which shines [like a beautiful] flower’)
------------------------------------------
Whether the science of aeronautics was known to the ancient Hindus or not, पुष्पक or Puṣpakavimāna, the most wonderful aeroplane—the like of which never existed earlier nor would, in future—has often been mentioned in the Hindu scriptural works.
The पुष्पक originally belonged to कुबेर, the god of wealth. It had been given to him by none other than ब्रह्मा, the creator himself, as a gift. It had been manufactured by विश्वकर्म, the chief architect and engineer of the gods in हेअवेन्. It was extraordinarily elegant, highly decorated, could accommodate any number of people by expanding (and contracting) and could fly independently at the ‘speed of मिन्द्’ (manovega)!
Rāvaṇa, the demon-king, had usurped it from कुबेर (his own cousin!) after conquering him in the battle.
When राम killed रावण, विभीषण offered the पुष्पक to him to return to अयोध्या (vide Rāmāyaṇa, Yuddhakāṇḍa, 124.9-12). When राम wanted कुबेर, the original owner, to take it back, the latter gifted it to राम himself.
Rāma then ordered the पुष्पक to move about freely at will, but to return to him whenever he wanted it.
In the Sundarakāṇḍa of वाल्मीकि’s Rāmāyaṇa (sargas 7 and 8) there is a beautiful and captivating description of this पुष्पक, as seen by हनुमान्.

Puṣya
(‘the flower’)
------------------------------------------
It is the eighth नक्षत्र or constellation comprising the स्तर्स् gamma, delta and theta Cancri.
Bṛhaspati or गुरु is its presiding deity. It belongs to the zodiacal sign Karkāṭaka (Cancer). One who is born under this star will be ‘handsome, devoted to his parents and will specialise in theatrical arts’.
Most of the सṁस्कारस् like nāma-karaṇa (naming ceremony), उपनयन (investiture with the sacred thread), विवाह (marriage), गृहप्रवेश (dedicating and entering a new होउसे) are performed during the presence of this नक्षत्र in the day.

Puṣkara
------------------------------------------
The town of पुष्कर situated at a distance of 12 kms. (about 7 1/2 miles) to the west of Ajmer in Rajasthan and on the bank of the lake of the same name, has the unique distinction of possessing a good temple—the only one in the whole of India—dedicated to ब्रह्मा, the creator.
The greatness of पुष्कर as an excellent place of पिल्ग्रिमगे has been extolled in many पुराणस् as also the epics (vide Mahābhārata, Vanaparva 80.20, 21); Padmapurāṇa, Ādikhaṇḍa 11.34, 35).
Once while ब्रह्मा, the creator, was moving in a forest with a lotus in his hand, he found a rākṣasa (demon), Vajranābha by name, whom he killed with his lotus, after converting it into a formidable weapon through mantras or sacred chants. Hence that place—the present Puṣkara—came to be known as पुष्कर (= lotus).
The same legend says that the lotus in his hand rebounded at three places before killing the demon. All these three places became lakes, respectively known as Jyeṣṭha-पुष्कर, Madhya-पुष्कर and Kaniṣṭha-पुष्कर. The presiding deities of these three are ब्रह्मा, विष्णु and रुद्र.
At the Jyeṣṭa-पुष्कर ब्रह्मा is said to have performed a यज्ञ or a sacrifice. Hence animals are not allowed to be killed in this area.
The greatest festival of पुष्कर is held on the Kārttika Pūrṇimā day (generally in November). Lakhs of pilgrims gather here on that day to take bath in the main lake and worship ब्रह्मा.
The main temple is that of the four-faced ब्रह्मा, the creator. It is situated very near the main lake. The image of ब्रह्मा is in the centre and the images of his two spouses—Sāvitrī and Gāyatrī—are on his right and left sides. The temple has the images of the four sages सनक, Sanandana, Sanatkumāra and Sanatsujāta also.
The other temples in पुष्कर are those of नारद (the divine sage), Badarī-नारायण, Varāha, शिव (known as Ātmeśvara-महादेव), Ramā-वैकुण्ठ or Śrī Raṅgajī, Venugopāla and Śrī राम.
Other important places of पिल्ग्रिमगे are the Yajñaparvata, the hermitage of अगस्त्य, and five kuṇḍas (small ponds) of which the Nāgakuṇḍa appears to be more well-known.
Going round the whole place (called parikrama) has been considered as a holy act. Some pilgrims undertake that arduous task in which they have to walk from 10 to 77 kms. (6 to 48 miles), depending on the type they choose.
There is a river सरस्वती here that flows in five streams.

puṣṭimārgā
------------------------------------------
Teachers of the भक्ति Movement made religion not only simple but also affable, by their inspiring lives and simple teachings.
One such teacher who wielded consi-derable influence over a large section of people was Vallabhācārya or वल्लभ (A. D. 1473-1531.)
The words ‘puṣṭi’ and ‘puṣṭimārga’ are his contribution to the भक्ति literature.
He categorises भक्ति or devotion to God into ‘maryādābhakti’ and ‘puṣṭi-भक्ति’.
The devotion that follows the beaten track as per the various steps given in the scriptures like śravaṇa (listening to the glories of God), कीर्तन (singing devotional songs) and arcana (worship) belongs to the first category. The jīvas (souls) or sādhakas (aspirants) who follow this path have to depend much on self-effort.
Puṣṭimārga is the path of devotion categorised as ‘puṣṭi’.
‘Puṣṭi’ literally means ‘nourishment’. It means the special spiritual nourishment that a sādhaka gets when God’s grace descends on him. It has nothing to do with the fattening of the body with nourishing ड़ोओद्, as some epicureans want us to believe!
In this path, the जीव on whom the grace of God falls, is called ‘puṣṭi’. He is the one whom God has accepted as his own. These jīvas have an innate and unconditional love and attachment to him. That love is actually a reflection of the light of divine favour and fervour on that blessed सोउल्.
Well-known scriptures on भक्ति or devotion advocate navavidha-भक्ति or ninefold devotion. They are: śravaṇa (listening to the stories of God in his various aspects of avatāras), कीर्तन (singing his names and glories), smaraṇa (remembering him constantly), pādasevana (serving the feet of his images), arcana (ritualistic worship), vandana (obeisance to him), dāsya (cultivating the attitude that one is his servant), sakhya (an attitude of friendship towards him) and ātmanivedana (offering oneself completely to him or total self-surrender) (vide Bhāgavata 7.5.23).
The first eight modes belong to the mode of maryādā-भक्ति. In the puṣṭimārga, the devotee starts with the last mode (ātmanivedana). Realising that the grace of God is the sole means of achieving spiritual progress, he gets the मन्त्र of self-dedication from a qualified गुरु in a ceremony called ‘brahma-sambandha.’ This absolves him of all his past sins even as the river गङ्गा purifies all the dirty water that may flow into it.
Of course, the efficacy of such an initiation depends on the intensity of the faith and aspiration of the disciple.
See also VALLABHĀCĀRYA.
